fields.foundation: The Ashanti Empire, more properly the Asante Empire, was founded around the turn of the eighteenth century, when Osei Tutu I deliberately united the fragmented Akan chiefdoms of the forest zone of modern Ghana in a political and spiritual union. At the time the Asante states of the interior were subject to Denkyira, a powerful forest kingdom to the south-west. They paid it tribute, and it controlled their access to the coast and to European trade goods, particularly firearms obtained through the Dutch at Elmina. Osei Tutu, of the Oyoko clan, became ruler of the small state of Kumasi in the later seventeenth century (traditionally around 1680). He recognised that while they were divided the Asante could not challenge Denkyira, and he allied himself with the priest Okomfo Anokye, whose summoning of the Golden Stool from the heavens became the most powerful founding tradition in Asante history. The Golden Stool (Sika Dwa Kofi), said to have descended from the sky amid thunder and a cloud of white dust to rest on Osei Tutu's knees, was declared to hold the soul of the Asante nation. It bound the member states to a single loyalty that stood above allegiance to individual chiefs. Okomfo Anokye is traditionally credited with promulgating the laws and customs of the new union, remembered as the Seventy-Seven Laws, and with establishing the Odwira festival as an annual rite of national unity. The first military test came at the Battle of Feyiase in 1701, where the Asante coalition defeated Denkyira, killing its king Ntim Gyakari and taking over the Dutch rent note for Elmina. This gave Asante direct access to coastal European trade and to the firearms that drove its later expansion. Kumasi became the capital of the new union, and Osei Tutu its first Asantehene.
fields.socioeconomy: The Asante imperial economy was based on the gold fields of the Akan forest zone, among the richest alluvial and reef gold deposits in West Africa. It grew through a varied trade network linking the forest interior to the Atlantic coast and to the Saharan routes to the north. Gold, kola nuts and captives were the empire's principal exports: gold for the European coastal trade; kola nuts for Muslim communities across the Sahel, who valued them as a stimulant permitted under Islamic law; and captives sold both into the Atlantic trade and northwards. Control of the main routes between the coast and the interior was a lasting advantage. Merchants moving goods between the forest and the Atlantic ports passed through territory where the Asantehene could levy tolls and regulate commerce, and from 1807 Kumasi increasingly turned northwards, sending kola to the great markets of Salaga and Hausaland. Gold dust was the currency, weighed with distinctive brass weights, and specialist officials managed the Great Treasury in Kumasi under a developed system of royal accounting; when British forces entered the palace in 1874 they found gold and also books and manuscripts in several languages. Asante society was built on matrilineal descent and a hierarchy of chiefs, priests, military commanders and royal officials. The reforms traditionally associated with Osei Kwadwo (r. 1764–1777), who promoted officials to central offices on the basis of ability and service rather than birth, helped to turn the empire from an aristocratic confederation into a more bureaucratic polity able to administer its growing territory. The slave trade was economically significant, but it also tied the empire to European firearms, and this dependence limited its freedom of action in later confrontations with British power.
fields.military: The Asante military combined a hierarchically organised army with a large capacity for mass mobilisation. Its command structure balanced royal authority with the fighting traditions of the member chiefdoms. The army was organised in divisions, with an advance guard, a main body around the commander, two wings and a rearguard, each led by chiefs of the constituent states commanding their own contingents under the overall direction of the Asantehene's generals. European observers reported Asante armies of tens of thousands in the field during the campaigns of Opoku Ware I (r. c. 1720–1750), who conquered Bono, Gyaman and the southern parts of Gonja. Such numbers were exceptional for the region. The systematic use of firearms, obtained first through the Dutch at Elmina and later through several coastal trading relationships, gave the Asante a decisive edge over interior peoples who lacked coastal access. The empire's most celebrated victory came on 21 January 1824 at the Battle of Nsamankow, where an Asante army annihilated a British-led force under Governor Sir Charles MacCarthy, who was killed; his skull was reputedly kept in Kumasi as a trophy. The victory showed that the Asante could defeat European-led forces in forest warfare, where terrain partly cancelled an advantage in firepower. Over time, however, the Anglo-Ashanti Wars exposed the empire's limits. Britain could bring artillery, rockets, logistics and professional troops to bear in coordinated campaigns, above all Sir Garnet Wolseley's 1874 expedition, which fought its way to Kumasi and burned it despite fierce resistance at Amoaful and Odasu. In the end these overwhelmed a military system built for regional warfare rather than for a long contest with an industrial power.
fields.governance: The Asante system of government was among the most developed constitutional arrangements in pre-colonial Africa, and it combined sacred monarchical authority with institutional checks on royal power. The Asantehene exercised supreme authority but governed in consultation with the Asantemanhyiamu, the national assembly of the paramount chiefs of the member states, and, in the nineteenth century, with the Kotoko Council, an inner council of senior chiefs and officials in Kumasi; their assent was expected for major decisions, including war and peace, and an Asantehene could himself be destooled. The Golden Stool was at once a religious object, a constitutional symbol and a practical limit on royal authority: no one sat on it, and the Asantehene was enstooled beneath it, acknowledging that his authority derived from the collective soul of the nation rather than from personal right. Kumasi impressed European visitors. The British envoy Thomas Bowdich, who visited in 1817, described broad, clean streets, houses ornamented with elaborate relief decoration, disciplined troops and court ceremonies of great splendour. The administrative reforms associated with Osei Kwadwo and his successors created appointed offices, including resident commissioners in provincial states, that strengthened the centre's capacity to govern. The empire ruled the Asante heartland directly and held its outer provinces through tributary arrangements, under which chiefs acknowledged Asante suzerainty, paid tribute and supplied military contingents. In the colonial era this system was a strength and a weakness. Its institutions proved very resilient, so that the Golden Stool was never surrendered and the Asante kingship survives as a recognised traditional authority within Ghana today, but it also limited the empire's capacity to concentrate the resources needed for total mobilisation against British imperialism.
fields.impact: The Asante Empire was one of West Africa's most powerful pre-colonial states, and its history also bears on African political thought, resistance to colonialism and the persistence of indigenous institutions into the modern world. Its armed resistance to British expansion lasted nearly eight decades and five Anglo-Asante wars between 1824 and 1900. It was among the longest sustained military resistance to British imperial expansion in Africa, and it showed that African political institutions could maintain organised resistance against European military technology for generations. The Battle of Nsamankow in 1824, in which MacCarthy's force was destroyed, was one of the heaviest defeats suffered by British forces in West Africa. It shook British confidence and was followed by a period in which the British government considered abandoning its Gold Coast forts and handed their administration to a committee of merchants, and British policy towards Asante was more cautious for decades. Economically, Asante joined the Akan gold fields to both Atlantic and Saharan trade networks and so influenced the commercial geography of West Africa for nearly two centuries, building on a gold trade that had already given the Gold Coast its European name long before Asante arose. Culturally, Adinkra symbols, kente weaving, goldwork and brass gold-weights, and the political philosophy expressed in the Golden Stool have become internationally recognised expressions of Akan civilisation. The Asante kingship survives as a living institution within the Republic of Ghana, where the Asantehene is recognised as a traditional ruler whose authority in customary matters is protected by the Ghanaian constitution. It is a rare instance of a pre-colonial African political institution that continued through colonial annexation and into the post-independence era.
fields.decline: The Asante Empire did not collapse suddenly, as many other pre-colonial African states did. It declined in steps, through successive military defeats and the growing pressure of British colonial power. The first serious check came at the Battle of Katamansu in 1826, where a British-led coalition of coastal peoples, aided by Congreve rockets, defeated an Asante army that had advanced to the coast after the Nsamankow victory. The 1831 Treaty of Peace, negotiated by George Maclean, recognised the River Pra as the effective southern boundary of Asante influence and permanently curtailed the empire's ambitions on the coast. The decisive blow came in the Third Anglo-Ashanti War of 1873–1874, when Sir Garnet Wolseley led a force built around some 2,500 British regulars, with West Indian and African troops, into Asante territory, entered Kumasi on 4 February 1874, looted the palace and burned the capital two days later. The Treaty of Fomena that followed required Asante to pay an indemnity of 50,000 ounces of gold, renounce claims to the southern states and Elmina, and end human sacrifice. It also encouraged several former tributaries to break away, which broke up the empire's provincial network and set off civil strife. In 1896, in the Fourth Anglo-Ashanti War, a British expedition occupied Kumasi without a fight and deposed Asantehene Prempeh I, who was exiled first to Sierra Leone and from 1900 to the Seychelles. The final act of resistance came in 1900, when Yaa Asantewaa, Queen Mother of Ejisu, led the War of the Golden Stool, one of the last major armed risings against British rule in West Africa, after Governor Sir Frederic Hodgson demanded that the Golden Stool be surrendered to him. The rising was crushed by the end of the year and Yaa Asantewaa was exiled to the Seychelles. On 1 January 1902 Asante was formally annexed as a British crown colony, yet the Golden Stool remained hidden and was never captured. In 1935 the British restored the Asante Confederacy under Prempeh II.
fields.summary: The Asante Empire had two centuries of military and political success, and its institutions survived its defeat. The Golden Stool was never surrendered, and the Asantehene remains a constitutionally recognised traditional ruler within Ghana today. The Asante kingship is one of the very few pre-colonial African political institutions to have lasted from the late seventeenth century to the present.
fields.teaser: The Ashanti Confederacy of Ghana was known for its wealth in gold and the sacred Golden Stool, symbol of the nation's soul. Their resistance to British colonialism was fierce and prolonged.
fields.t0: Osei Tutu I united Akan chiefdoms in Ghana's forest zone around 1700, bound together by the sacred Golden Stool.
fields.t1: Rich in gold and kola, Asante resisted British expansion through five wars between 1824 and 1900.
fields.t2: Annexed by Britain in 1902, it never surrendered the Golden Stool, and its king is still recognised in Ghana today.
fields.dyk: No one sits on the Golden Stool: the Asantehene is enstooled beneath it, as it embodies the soul of the whole Asante nation.
